traveler: The Comte de Saint-Germain (Weldon, Tzarogy, Zurmont, Aymar, Surmont)
title: The Man Without a Birth: from the Sloane Letter to the Eckernforde Register
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Sarospatak Castle, the Rakoczi hypothesis
stops.date_confidence: legend, wholly undated; no birth, baptism, or guardianship record connects the documented adventurer to the Rakoczi family. The date is an ordering device only and rests on nothing. Carried by Cooper-Oakley and Jean Overton Fuller; the dossier's own lead could not corroborate it from any outside source.
stops.campa: Occult genealogy gives him a cradle here, in the seat of the Rakoczi princes of Transylvania, and makes him an unacknowledged son of Francis II Rakoczi, hidden abroad while the family estates stood forfeit. No birth entry, no baptism, no guardianship account, no household expense ties the man who later signs himself Saint-Germain to that dynasty. The name Tzarogy, which he uses at the court of Ansbach some eighty years afterwards, is Ragotzy read backwards. That reversal is the whole of the case. Cooper-Oakley prints the descent in 1912 and Jean Overton Fuller prints it again in 1988.
suggested_refs: The Rakoczi seat at Sarospatak, dynastic anchor of the count's legendary parentage
sources: Isabel Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain: The Secret of Kings (1912)
Jean Overton Fuller, The Comte de Saint-Germain: Last Scion of the House of Rakoczy (1988)
Dictionary of Gnosis and Western Esotericism (Brill), entry 'Saint-Germain'

stops.name: Palazzo Pitti, Florence: the childhood he describes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1712 birth year comes from a Brussels Gazette notice reprinted in Read's Weekly Journal, 17 May 1760, a press report and not a civil record; the Medici household story rests on Charles of Hesse-Kassel's Memoires de mon temps (1861), reporting the count's own account decades after the fact. Month and day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He tells Prince Charles of Hesse-Kassel, late in life, that he was raised in Florence in the household of Gian Gastone de' Medici, last grand duke of the line, on the money of a birth nobody would acknowledge. A press notice out of Brussels, reprinted in London in 1760, gives the same country and a year, 1712, and no parish. Later biographies add an education at the University of Siena for which no matriculation register has ever been produced. Every account of his childhood comes from him or from a newspaper. Not one of them is older than 1760, by which time he is already famous.
suggested_refs: Charles of Hesse-Kassel, Memoires de mon temps (Copenhagen, 1861), the count's own account of his origins
Read's Weekly Journal or British Gazetteer, 17 May 1760
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.22
Brill, Dictionary of Gnosis and Western Esotericism, 'Saint-Germain'

stops.name: The Hague, the letter to Sir Hans Sloane
stops.date_confidence: contested. Cooper-Oakley's list of illustrations gives a letter of 1735; her own chapter contents give 1733 for the same document. The pool's '22 November 1735' and its Wikipedia citation could not be substantiated: the English Wikipedia article contains no Sloane letter and no shelfmark. The addressee cannot have been the British Museum, which was founded in 1753. Sloane MS 4026, fols. 289r-290v unverified against any catalogue.
stops.campa: A man signing himself de Saint-Germain writes from The Hague to Sir Hans Sloane in London, offering an incunable to the greatest private collector in Europe. Sloane's papers pass at his death into the founding collection of the British Museum, which is why the letter is catalogued under the Museum's name and dated by one page of the same book to 1733 and by another to 1735. It is the first piece of paper in the world that bears him. He is at this point a bookseller's correspondent. Nobody has yet written down what he looks like or how old he is.
suggested_refs: The Sloane manuscripts in the British Library, founding collection of the British Museum
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), list of illustrations and ch. II contents
Brill, Dictionary of Gnosis and Western Esotericism, 'Saint-Germain'

segments.name: England and Vienna: the First Documents

stops.name: King's Theatre, Haymarket: the arias in L'Incostanza delusa
stops.date_confidence: attested. The pasticcio ran on all but one of the Saturdays from 9 February to 20 April 1745, not continuously as a date range implies. The pin is the King's Theatre site, now His Majesty's Theatre at Haymarket and Charles II Street; the pool's -0.1348 falls a block west on Lower Regent Street and is not used.
stops.campa: Arias credited to him are sung in the pasticcio L'Incostanza delusa at the King's Theatre, on all but one of the Saturdays between the ninth of February and the twentieth of April. Whoever he is, he can write for professional singers, and a London opera management pays to have his music heard by a paying house. The manuscript of Italian arias he calls Musique raisonnee belongs to the same craft, a hand any copyist can grade. He has been living in England two years by the time the run opens.
suggested_refs: The Musique raisonnee manuscript of Italian arias
His Majesty's Theatre, Haymarket, on the site of the King's Theatre of 1745
sources: Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'
Wikipedia, "His Majesty's Theatre, London"

stops.name: London, seized in the Jacobite winter
stops.date_confidence: attested by Walpole's letter to Sir Horace Mann of 9 December 1745, printed in the 1833 edition of the letters and quoted verbatim by Cooper-Oakley, p.22. The German Wikipedia treats this letter as the first secure report of the count's existence, which would put the 1735 Hague letter in question. The precise London address is not recorded and the pin is the city.
stops.campa: With Charles Edward Stuart's army marching south and every foreigner in London under suspicion, the authorities take up a man calling himself Count St. Germain. He tells them plainly that the name is not his own and declines to supply another. They find nothing to charge him with and let him go, and no record of the interrogation survives beyond the fact of it. Horace Walpole, writing to Horace Mann on the ninth of December, notes the release, the violin, and the two years the man has already spent in England.
stops.quote: The other day they seized an odd man who goes by the name of Count St. Germain. He has been here these two years, and will not tell who he is or whence, but professes that he does not go by his right name. He sings and plays on the violin wonderfully, is mad, and not very sensible.
stops.quote_source: Horace Walpole to Sir Horace Mann, 9 December 1745, Letters of Horace Walpole to Sir Horace Mann, vol. ii, pp.108-109 (London, 1833)
suggested_refs: Walpole's correspondence with Sir Horace Mann, the earliest secure notice of the count
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.22
Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'
de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'

stops.name: Palais Lobkowitz, Vienna: the dedication of the arias
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and in open conflict with the London evidence. Van Sypesteyn's Historische Herinneringen (1869) puts him in Vienna 1745-46; Walpole has him in Britain through December 1745, and Ferdinand Philipp von Lobkowicz spent 1745 travelling to Italy and England with Gluck. Van Sypesteyn's 'first minister to Emperor Francis I' is false: Lobkowicz was 21 and held no ministry. Contradiction left standing.
stops.campa: Reports place him in Vienna living as a prince, under the protection of Ferdinand Philipp von Lobkowicz, twenty-one years old, a violinist who studies with Gluck and pays for music to be made. The arias of the Musique raisonnee carry a dedication to him. The chronology does not hold: Walpole has the count in Britain through December of 1745, and the young prince spends that year on the road to Italy and England. Van Sypesteyn, writing in 1869, is the only source for the Vienna residence, and he makes his patron a first minister he never was.
suggested_refs: Palais Lobkowitz, Vienna, seat of the prince to whom the Musique raisonnee is dedicated
sources: C. A. van Sypesteyn, Historische Herinneringen (The Hague, 1869), in Cooper-Oakley p.23 n.18
Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Philip, 6th Prince of Lobkowicz'

stops.name: Vienna, Marshal Belle-Isle takes him to Paris
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on a single late source, van Sypesteyn (1869), reported by Cooper-Oakley p.23 n.18. Month and day unknown and defaulted; the year follows the same Vienna residence whose dating is contested in the preceding stop.
stops.campa: Charles Louis Auguste Fouquet, duc de Belle-Isle, marshal of France, is in Vienna on Louis XV's business and meets the count in the circles that pass him from house to house. He is impressed enough to carry him back to Paris and open the court to him. Everything the count becomes in France runs through that carriage: without it, a musician with a false name; with it, a chemist lodged in a royal chateau at the king's expense. The story itself survives in one place, a Dutch memoir published a hundred and twenty years later, and van Sypesteyn does not say who told him.
suggested_refs: The letters of Marshal Belle-Isle that the count would still be producing at The Hague fourteen years later
sources: van Sypesteyn, Historische Herinneringen (1869), in Cooper-Oakley p.23 n.18

stops.name: Paris, admitted to the court of Louis XV
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline: the English Wikipedia has him appearing at the French court around 1748 and employed by Louis XV in 1749. The pool's chronology dated the court introduction to 1757, roughly a decade late, and is rejected. Month and day unknown and defaulted. Canonical Paris pin, inherited byte-identical from christian_rosenkreuz.journey.json and blavatsky.journey.json.
stops.campa: He appears at the French court around 1748 and is in Louis XV's employ by 1749, a man with no country, no family, and no rank, admitted because the king finds him interesting. He speaks the languages of every embassy in the city, plays the violin at private concerts, and talks about metals and dyes with the specificity of a workshop rather than a library. Madame de Pompadour receives him. What he does for his wages is never written into any surviving warrant, and this is a court that writes down the price of candles.
suggested_refs: The household accounts of Louis XV, which record the count's lodging but never his office
sources: Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'
de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'

stops.name: Versailles, the flawed diamond
stops.date_confidence: attested as an eyewitness memoir, not as a dated event. Madame du Hausset's Memoires were published in 1824, long after her death, and give no date for the episode; the year here follows Cooper-Oakley's placement of it in the count's early court period and is an ordering device. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Louis XV hands him a diamond with a visible flaw in it and asks whether anything can be done. A month later the stone comes back clean, and the king has it weighed and valued again and finds it worth more than it was. Madame du Hausset, chambermaid to Madame de Pompadour, is in the room and writes it down years afterwards in memoirs that are not printed until 1824. The stone is not described before or after by anyone else, and its later history is unknown. Whether the count improved it or exchanged it for another, nobody at Versailles asks out loud.
suggested_refs: Madame du Hausset, Memoires (Paris, 1824), p.148ff
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), pp.23-24

stops.name: Paris, Milord Gower plays the count
stops.date_confidence: attested as a Parisian episode by several independent memoirists (du Hausset, Barthold, Gleichen, van Sypesteyn) but undated by all of them; the year places it before Voltaire's letter of 15 April 1758, which already treats the Trent joke as current. Month and day defaulted. Canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: A Parisian mimic known as Milord Gower makes a salon turn of impersonating him, inventing on the spot the anecdotes the count himself never tells: intimacy with Richard the Lionheart, an evening at the Council of Trent, an opinion on the household of Pontius Pilate. Paris laughs, and within a season Paris has forgotten which stories came from which man. Voltaire, writing to Frederick the Great in April 1758, repeats the Trent joke as though it were the count's own boast. The immortality legend is built in a drawing room by a man doing an impression.
stops.quote: It is said to be only known by a M. de St. Germain, who supped formerly at Trent with the Council Fathers, and who will probably have the honour of seeing your Majesty in the course of fifty years. He is a man who never dies, and who knows everything.
stops.quote_source: Voltaire to Frederick the Great, 15 April 1758, Oeuvres de Voltaire, ed. Beuchot, letter cxviii, vol. lviii, p.360
suggested_refs: The memoirs of Baron de Gleichen and of Madame du Hausset, both naming the impersonator
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.24 and p.96 (1927 printing)

stops.name: Grand Trianon, the laboratory the king pays for
stops.date_confidence: place corrected, tag softened. The pool put this at the Petit Trianon for 1756-1760, which is impossible: the Petit Trianon's design was approved 20 May 1762, foundations laid at the end of that year, the building finished in 1768. German Wikipedia says only 'im Trianon-Schlosschen', which for this decade can only be the Grand Trianon of 1687. The laboratory itself is reported, not archivally attested, so this is [R] rather than [A].
stops.campa: The king fits out an alchemical laboratory for him at the Trianon, furnaces and glass at royal expense, and comes to watch him work, sometimes for hours. A foreigner whose birth nobody has established has fire and materials inside the enclosure of Versailles. The German account names only the Trianon Schlosschen, which in this decade can be no building but the Grand Trianon of 1687, the Petit Trianon being four years from its foundations. What comes out is dyes and colours and treated metals rather than gold, and no account book of the reign records a transmutation. The king keeps paying anyway.
suggested_refs: The Grand Trianon of 1687, the only Trianon standing in the 1750s
sources: de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'
Wikipedia, 'Petit Trianon'

stops.name: Chateau de Chambord, the rooms and the workshop
stops.date_confidence: attested by dated administrative correspondence reproduced in Cooper-Oakley, Appendix I, pp.74ff: letters of 10 May, 19 May, 12 August, 2 September 1758, with a further 4 December. German Wikipedia independently dates the grant of rooms at Chambord to 1758. The stop date is the first of the dated letters.
stops.campa: Letters run between the ministry and the chateau through the spring and summer about the count's apartment: rooms to be prepared, a workshop fitted out, servants lodged, dates of the tenth and nineteenth of May, the twelfth of August, the second of September. It is the most ordinary archive he leaves anywhere, quartermaster's correspondence about a man described elsewhere as immortal. What the letters arrange for is a suite of rooms, a laboratory, and a household expecting him. The royal manufactory that the legend builds at Chambord appears in none of them.
suggested_refs: Archives de l'Etat, Paris, correspondence on the count's apartment at Chambord, 1758
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), Appendix I, pp.74ff
de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'

stops.name: The Hague, the peace and the credit scheme
stops.date_confidence: attested by the d'Affry-Choiseul correspondence in Cooper-Oakley, Appendix II, pp.83ff, letters of 22 February, 10 March, 14 March 1760. English Wikipedia dates the journey to March 1760; the chronology lens gave February and the geography lens February-March. The stop takes the date of d'Affry's first dated report.
stops.campa: He arrives in the Dutch Republic at the height of the Seven Years' War carrying letters from Belle-Isle, and speaks to British and Dutch intermediaries about French finances, Dutch credit, and terms of peace, implying an authority from Louis XV that no minister has given him. The Comte d'Affry, France's ambassador, reports him to Choiseul on the twenty-second of February and again on the tenth and fourteenth of March. Nobody at the foreign ministry in Versailles had been told he was coming.
suggested_refs: The Choiseul-d'Affry correspondence, Cooper-Oakley Appendix II
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), Appendix II, pp.83ff
Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'

stops.name: The Hague, what he says about the king
stops.date_confidence: attested: Kauderbach's dispatch to Prince Galitzin is dated 14 March 1760 and is reproduced in Cooper-Oakley, Appendix VII, p.110. The quoted political speech survives only as Kauderbach's report of the count's words, not as an autograph; it is the closest thing to his own voice in any archive.
stops.campa: The Saxon minister at The Hague dines with him and writes to Prince Galitzin an account that mixes state business with wonder: a man charged with an important commission, known across Europe for his learning and his immense wealth, said to be over a hundred and ten years old and looking about forty-five. In the same conversations the count talks politics without flattery, naming the king's want of firmness and the financiers around him as the disease of France. Kauderbach writes the words down as he heard them, and no page in the count's own hand survives to be set beside them.
stops.quote: The radical evil is the monarch's want of firmness. Those who surround him, knowing his extreme good nature, abuse it, and he is surrounded only by creatures placed by the Brothers Paris, who alone cause all the trouble of France.
stops.quote_source: The count in conversation with M. de Kauderbach, The Hague, 1760, reported in Kauderbach's dispatch and quoted in Cooper-Oakley, p.48
suggested_refs: Kauderbach's dispatches from The Hague, Cooper-Oakley Appendix VII
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.48 and Appendix VII, p.110

stops.name: Versailles, Choiseul reads the despatch in council
stops.date_confidence: the scene is attested through Baron de Gleichen's Memoires, xi, pp.131-132, quoted at Cooper-Oakley p.99 of the 1927 printing, on the report of 'one present at the French Cabinet Council'. The location is inferred: Cooper-Oakley places the scene only 'in Council' and names no palace. The pool's page reference 'p.2031-area' is garbled and is replaced here. Month attested, day defaulted.
stops.campa: D'Affry's despatch reaches the Duc de Choiseul, who reads it aloud in council in front of Louis XV and Marshal Belle-Isle, together with the reply he has already sent ordering the count's arrest and extradition. Choiseul has caught his master running a private embassy behind the foreign ministry's back, and answers it by making the deniable agent undeniable. From this day the count is a man France has formally demanded be handed over. The king says nothing that anybody records.
stops.quote: If I did not give myself time to take the orders of the King, it is because I am convinced that no one here would be bold enough to desire to negotiate a Treaty of Peace without the knowledge of Your Majesty's Minister for Foreign Affairs!
stops.quote_source: The Duc de Choiseul to the French royal council, 1760, in Baron C. H. de Gleichen, Memoires, xi, pp.131-132, quoted in Cooper-Oakley p.99 (1927 printing)
suggested_refs: Gleichen's Memoires, the only account of the council scene
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912/1927), ch. 'Political Work', p.99

stops.name: Amsterdam, among the bankers
stops.date_confidence: attested for March 1760 by the English Wikipedia itinerary; the day is not fixed and is defaulted. The content of the scheme is known only through the diplomatic reports of men trying to work out what he was doing.
stops.campa: He moves to Amsterdam and lodges among the bankers, pressing the same combination of a peace and a loan, and the British and French residents both conclude that he is acting on an authority he will not name. Neither can discover whose. Behind him along the same roads the arrest order is travelling. He talks about French credit like a man who has seen the books, and whether anyone at Versailles ever opened them to him is a question no source in either archive answers.
suggested_refs: The Amsterdam banking houses approached in the spring of 1760
sources: Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'

stops.name: The Hague, the disappearance
stops.date_confidence: attested: M. Cornet's letter to the Count de Haslang is dated The Hague, 29 April 1760, and is reproduced in Cooper-Oakley pp.114-115. The Gazette of the Netherlands notice is datelined The Hague, 2 January 1761 and published 12 January 1761.
stops.campa: Three months in the country, a French demand for his arrest lodged with the States General, and then nothing: he is simply not where he was. M. Cornet writes to the Count de Haslang on the twenty-ninth of April that the foreigner whose origin and native country nobody knows has disappeared when it was least expected. The Dutch, who were never asked to protect him, decline to hunt him. The Gazette of the Netherlands will report the following January that he left without the king's leave and sent back his red ribbon.
stops.quote: A foreigner who calls himself the Comte de St. Germain, whose origin and native country no one knows, but who is said to be extremely rich and very well received at different Courts in Europe, especially at that of France, after a residence of about three months which he has made here, has just disappeared when it was least expected.
stops.quote_source: M. Cornet to the Count de Haslang, The Hague, 29 April 1760, in Cooper-Oakley, pp.114-115
suggested_refs: The Gazette of the Netherlands, 12 January 1761, on the returned red ribbon
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), pp.24, 114-115

stops.name: Hellevoetsluis, the passport made out in blank
stops.date_confidence: attested for May 1760 by the English Wikipedia and by the pool's own geography lens. The pool's chronology gave April and 'escapes across the Netherlands', which both understates the mechanism and contradicts the geography lens; the May date and the Bentinck-Yorke passport are preferred. Day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Willem Bentinck van Rhoon, who has taken a liking to him, gets a British passport out of Ambassador Joseph Yorke made out in blank, so that the man carrying it need not commit to paper which name he is using. Lord Holderness had instructed Yorke in March to demand authenticated proof of any royal authorization, and no such proof was ever produced. He sails from this port for London in May, out of reach of the French warrant. Eight weeks earlier he had been at The Hague as Louis XV's unofficial envoy.
suggested_refs: Sir Joseph Yorke's despatches and Lord Holderness's instructions of 21 and 28 March 1760, Cooper-Oakley Appendix III
sources: Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'
Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), Appendix III, pp.94ff

stops.name: London, the mysterious foreigner and the printed sonatas
stops.date_confidence: the London Chronicle account of 3 June 1760 is attested and cited by Cooper-Oakley p.24. The Walsh print of the six trio sonatas is undated: IMSLP gives 'n.d.' and does not support the pool's 1750s, nor does it claim the British Library exemplar is the only survivor. What IMSLP does confirm is 54 pages, a scan uploaded 27 March 2023, and no listed recordings or modern editions.
stops.campa: The London Chronicle of the third of June prints a long account of a mysterious foreigner newly landed on English shores, and the papers work backwards through the arrest of 1745 to make one figure out of two visits fifteen years apart. The city that took him up as a suspect in the Jacobite winter now reads about him over breakfast. He stays in England until 1762. John Walsh prints six trio sonatas under his name; the exemplar scanned from the British Library carries no date, has no modern edition, and lists no recording.
suggested_refs: Six Sonatas for Two Violins with a Bass, printed by John Walsh, London, undated, scanned by the British Library
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.24
imslp.org, '6 Trio Sonatas (Comte de Saint-Germain)'

segments.name: Dyes, Debts, and a Coup He May Not Have Attended

stops.name: Ubbergen, near Nijmegen: the laboratory in the house
stops.date_confidence: attested: Hardenbroeck's diary entry of 20 March 1762, Historisch Genootschap of Utrecht edition, vol. i, p.220, translated in Cooper-Oakley's appendix, p.101. German Wikipedia dates the purchase of the estate near Nijmegen to 1763 and the departure to August of that year with considerable debts left behind, which does not sit easily with a Dutch diary already describing the laboratory in March 1762. Contradiction left standing. Coordinates corrected to Ubbergen proper.
stops.campa: He buys an estate outside Nijmegen and fits a laboratory into the house, shutting himself in for whole days at a time and coming out with colours: leather, wool, cloth dyed in shades that Dutch visitors call the loveliest imaginable. Hardenbroeck records it in a diary entry of March 1762, together with land the count also holds near Zutphen. The chemistry is real and the colours are real. The business is not, and when he goes out of the Netherlands he leaves considerable debts behind him.
stops.quote: he also owns some landed property near Zutphen; that he has a huge laboratory in his house in which he shuts himself up for whole days at a time; that he knows how to bestow the most lovely colours imaginable on things, for instance on leather, etc.; that he is a great philosopher and lover of Nature; a fine conversationalist.
stops.quote_source: Memoirs of Hardenbroeck, Historisch Genootschap of Utrecht ed., vol. i, p.220, entry for 20 March 1762, translated in Cooper-Oakley, Appendix, p.101
suggested_refs: The estate at Ubbergen and its dye laboratory, described by Hardenbroeck
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), Appendix, p.101
de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'

stops.name: Zutphen, the land on the IJssel
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1762 by the German Wikipedia itinerary; the day is not recorded and is defaulted. Hardenbroeck's March entry independently confirms that he held property near Zutphen at this period.
stops.campa: He is recorded in this small Gelderland town in the summer of 1762, holding property here as well as at Ubbergen, in the middle of a two-year back-and-forth across the Republic that no single source follows all the way through. The Dutch years are the best documented stretch of his life and the least dramatic: purchases, laboratories, dye trials, creditors. He is trying to convert a court reputation into a manufactory. No manufactory is ever recorded.
suggested_refs: The Gelderland property records of the early 1760s
sources: de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'
Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), Appendix, p.101

stops.name: Winter Palace, Saint Petersburg: the coup he is said to have made
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and unsupported by any Russian record. The Orlov remark reaches print only in Curiositaten der Literarisch-historischen Vor- und Mitwelt (Weimar, 1818), pp.285-286, decades later and at second hand. Cooper-Oakley's counter-evidence, a stay with Princess Golitsyna at Arkhangelskoye on 3 March 1762, is itself unsourced in her text and conflicts with Dutch records for the same spring. No state paper, payment, or eyewitness places him in Russia.
stops.campa: Catherine takes the Russian throne from her husband in July, and later writers put the count inside the palace revolution that did it, on the word of Count Orlov, who is said to have told the Margrave of Ansbach that Saint-Germain played a great part in it. No Russian state paper names him, no payment records him, no witness sets him in the city. Cooper-Oakley answers the objection by putting him with Princess Golitsyna at Arkhangelskoye in March, which does not help, since Dutch records have him in Gelderland that same spring.
suggested_refs: Alexander Pushkin, The Queen of Spades (1834), which fixes the count in Russian literary memory as the keeper of three winning cards
Curiositaten der Literarisch-historischen Vor- und Mitwelt (Weimar, 1818), pp.285-286
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), pp.20, 24
Brill, Dictionary of Gnosis and Western Esotericism, 'Saint-Germain'
Neil Cornwell, New Zealand Slavonic Journal (2002), on Pushkin's use of the count

stops.name: Amsterdam, the return and the vanishing
stops.date_confidence: attested for August 1762 by the German Wikipedia itinerary; day defaulted. This stop and the preceding one cannot both be true as usually told, and neither source acknowledges the other's existence.
stops.campa: He is in Amsterdam again in August and then he is not in the Netherlands at all; he goes out of the country the way he went out of The Hague two years before, quickly and owing money. The estate near Nijmegen stays behind him, and the creditors file their claims against it. No Dutch source follows him past the border, and none of them says where he went. In the same season, later memoirists will place him inside a palace revolution two thousand miles east of the notaries who are writing his name down here.
suggested_refs: The Dutch creditors' claims following his departure in 1762-63
sources: de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'

stops.name: Brussels, Cobenzl watches the experiments
stops.date_confidence: attested: Count Karl Cobenzl to Chancellor Kaunitz, dated Brussels, 8 April 1763, quoted in full in Cooper-Oakley pp.24-25 and corroborated by the Austrian State Archives holding cited in the dossier lead. The India claim in the same paragraph rests on a letter attributed to the count and addressed to Count Maximilian von Lamberg, undated in Cooper-Oakley and uncorroborated by any ship's list.
stops.campa: Count Karl Cobenzl, minister plenipotentiary for Austria in the Netherlands, watches him work and writes to Chancellor Kaunitz what he has seen with his own eyes: iron turned into a metal as good as gold, skins and wool dyed in brilliant colours at a fraction of the usual cost, ultramarine improved. He mentions that the count is arranging a works at Tournai under the name M. de Zurmont. To Lamberg the same count explains his skill with jewels by a second journey to India in 1755 with General Clive and Admiral Watson, which no ship's list confirms.
stops.quote: I found him the most singular man that I ever saw in my life. I do not yet precisely know his birth; I believe, however, that he is the son of a clandestine union in a powerful and illustrious family. Possessing great wealth, he lives in the greatest simplicity; he knows everything, and shows an uprightness, a goodness of soul, worthy of admiration.
stops.quote_source: Count Karl Cobenzl to Prince Kaunitz, Brussels, 8 April 1763, quoted in Cooper-Oakley, pp.24-25
suggested_refs: The Cobenzl-Kaunitz correspondence in the Austrian State Archives
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), pp.24-25
Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'

stops.name: Tournai, Casanova at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1763 through Casanova's Memoires, vol. vi, p.76, as quoted and partly paraphrased in Cooper-Oakley p.24; month and day are not given and are defaulted. Cooper-Oakley renders the passage in indirect discourse, so the wording quoted here is hers reporting Casanova, not a certified translation of the Histoire de ma vie. The French original could not be consulted.
stops.campa: Casanova, travelling toward Tournai, hears that the count is there and asks to be presented. The answer comes back that he receives nobody; a written request then gets him an interview on two conditions, that he come incognito and that he not be offered food at the count's table. Both conditions are met. Casanova, who has talked his way into most of the courts of Europe, is received at a table where he is not allowed to eat, by a man dressed as an Armenian with a long beard, who is in the town to set up Cobenzl's factory.
stops.quote: Casanova on the road to Tournay was informed of the presence of M. le Comte de St. Germain, and desired to be presented to him. Being told that the Comte received no one, he wrote him to request an interview, which was granted under the restriction of coming incognito, and not being invited to partake of food with him. Casanova found the Comte in the dress of an Armenian with a long beard.
stops.quote_source: Casanova, Memoires, vol. vi, p.76, as quoted and paraphrased in Cooper-Oakley, p.24
suggested_refs: Casanova, Histoire de ma vie, the Tournai interview
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.24

segments.name: The German Courts and the Changing Names

stops.name: Livorno, Count Lamberg and the Orlov brothers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Livorno stay with Lamberg is reported in Lamberg's travel narratives, which could not be fetched directly. The English Wikipedia itinerary gives Venice as a single year, 1769, not the pool's 'circa 1765-1769', and the alias Aymar for Venice could not be corroborated. The Nuremberg meeting of 1772 is from the German Wikipedia. Month and day defaulted throughout.
stops.campa: The Italian years leave almost no archive: a notice for Venice in 1769, a report datelined Tunis that reaches a Florentine paper in July 1770, and this, that he is at Livorno in the company of Count Maximilian von Lamberg while Alexei Orlov's fleet is in the Mediterranean. The acquaintance with Orlov is real and begins here, eight years after the coup it is later produced to prove. Lamberg's own travel narratives carry the Livorno stay, and nothing else corroborates it. The two meet again at Nuremberg in 1772.
suggested_refs: Notizie del Mondo, Florence, July 1770, dateline Tunis
Lamberg's travel narratives of the Italian years
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.28 n.
de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'
Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'

stops.name: The Hague, the third visit
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1774 by the German Wikipedia itinerary and by Cooper-Oakley, whose sentence reads that the count came to The Hague after the death of Louis XV on 10 May 1774. The pool's chronology sent him to Bad Schwalbach on the strength of the same page, which contradicts both its own geography lens and Cooper-Oakley's wording. Month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: Louis XV dies on the tenth of May, and the count comes back to The Hague: the city of his first surviving letter, of his best chance and his worst failure, entered now for the third time by a man in his sixties whose protector is dead. Cooper-Oakley puts him here after the king's death; the same passage is often quoted as sending him instead to Bad Schwalbach. He passes through Mantua and Lausanne in this stretch of travelling. Nothing in it looks like a plan.
suggested_refs: The Hague, seat of the 1735 letter, the 1760 mission, and this last return
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.28
de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'

stops.name: Schloss Triesdorf, Ansbach: the name Tzarogy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1774-1776 by the German Wikipedia; Cooper-Oakley gives the same court visit at pp.29-30 and the pool's chronology dated it 1776, the geography lens 1774-1776. The stop takes the opening of the range. Month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: At the country seat of Karl Alexander, Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach, he presents himself as Tzarogy and offers chemistry, medicines, and a genealogy. The margrave is curious for the better part of two years and then is not. He leaves with no office, no capital, and nobody persuaded, and the name goes back into the bag with the others: Zurmont, Aymar, Welldone, Weldon, Surmont, Montferrat. Each is a real signature on a real receipt in a different town.
suggested_refs: Schloss Triesdorf, summer seat of the Margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach
sources: de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'
Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), pp.29-30

stops.name: Berlin, the mystery Frederick does not solve
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1776 by the English Wikipedia itinerary; month and day unknown and defaulted. The correspondence involving Frederick the Great and Princess Anna Amalia records curiosity about his origins and his claimed Masonic grades, not any royal endorsement. The Hamburg and Brunswick material is dated 1776-1778 by the German Wikipedia and is folded into this stop rather than given one of its own.
stops.campa: Frederick the Great, who has been hearing about him for twenty years from Voltaire and from everyone else, has his origins inquired into, and Princess Anna Amalia's circle probes the Masonic grades he is understood to hold. Nobody can verify a grade. What the Berlin correspondence records is curiosity about where he came from, and no endorsement of any kind. At Hamburg the Duke of Brunswick's brethren inquire in the same years and reach the same result. Frederick's own line is that the man is a mystery which has never been solved.
suggested_refs: The Berlin correspondence on the count's origins and grades, involving Frederick II and Princess Anna Amalia
sources: Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'
de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'

stops.name: Leipzig, Herr von Welldone
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1776 through the correspondence quoted in Cooper-Oakley p.68 (Bjornstahl, Reise in Europa, and letters of 1776-77); Chamberlain Dubosc's letter is dated 15 March 1777. Day of arrival not recorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: He arrives in October under the name v. Welldone and offers secret processes to whoever will pay for them, chemical, technical, industrial, the same catalogue he has been carrying since Brussels. He is somewhere in his sixties, running a workshop out of a travelling case. Every letter that survives about him from these years is written by an official deciding whether he is worth an interview. Chamberlain Dubosc writes one of them to a correspondent on the fifteenth of March following.
suggested_refs: Bjornstahl, Reise in Europa (1774), vol. V, and the 1776-77 Saxon correspondence
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.68
de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'

stops.name: Dresden, the file passed between ministers
stops.date_confidence: attested: Minister von Wurmb writes from Dresden on 19 May 1777, with related letters from Leipzig on 8 May 1777 and Gimmern on 3 June 1777, all quoted in Cooper-Oakley pp.68-69. The letters themselves were not consulted in the original.
stops.campa: Von Wurmb's letter of the nineteenth of May belongs to a small correspondence, Leipzig on the eighth of May, Gimmern on the third of June, in which Saxon officials pass the count between them like a file. The word they keep reaching for is not fraud. It is undecidable. He offers them processes that work, prices that do not, and an account of himself that nobody can check, and each of them writes to the next asking what should be made of it. None of the letters records an answer.
suggested_refs: The Saxon ministerial correspondence of May and June 1777
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), pp.68-69

stops.name: Schloss Wilhelmsbad, Hanau: the congress he is said to attend
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; participant lists have not been checked against the claim. The Convent of the Strict Observance met at Wilhelmsbad in the summer of 1782 for roughly fifty days with about thirty-five delegates, which is firm. The pool's chronology dated a Wilhelmsbad appearance to 15 February 1785 on the strength of Latomia vol. ii, p.9: that date belongs to the Convent des Philalethes at Paris, and the two assemblies have been fused. Coordinates corrected to the spa park. Month attested, day defaulted.
stops.campa: Masonic tradition puts him at the great congress of the Strict Observance in the spa park at Wilhelmsbad, fifty days of German lodges arguing through the summer over whether their higher degrees descend from the Templars or from nobody at all. He is by then living in Holstein under the protection of a Danish prince, and no participant list produced so far carries his name. A related tradition has him invited to the Convent of the Philalethes at Paris in February 1785, which falls ten months after his funeral.
suggested_refs: The Convent of Wilhelmsbad, summer 1782, and its surviving delegate lists
sources: de.wikipedia, 'Wilhelmsbad'
Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.64, citing Latomia vol. ii, p.9

stops.name: Altona, the friendship with Prince Charles of Hesse-Kassel
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1778-1779, with the two Wikipedias disagreeing: the German article dates the Schleswig arrival to 1778, the English to 1779. The Altona meeting itself is dated 1778-1779 by the German article. Month and day unknown and defaulted. The quoted judgement is Cooper-Oakley's English of Charles's French; the 1861 original was not checked.
stops.campa: In this Danish town beside Hamburg he meets Charles, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, royal governor of Schleswig, Freemason, and a man interested in exactly the things the count has to sell. Charles is not a mark. He is the one patron who keeps him to the end, gives him a house, a laboratory, and a burial, and writes about him afterwards in terms nobody used about him while he was still useful. The sources put the meeting in 1778 or in 1779; the friendship runs about five years either way.
stops.quote: He was, perhaps, one of the greatest philosophers who ever lived. The friend of humanity, wishing for money only that he might give to the poor, a friend to animals, his heart was concerned only with the happiness of others.
stops.quote_source: Charles, Prince of Hesse-Kassel, Memoires de Mon Temps (Copenhagen, 1861), p.135, in Cooper-Oakley's translation, p.9
suggested_refs: Charles of Hesse-Kassel, Memoires de mon temps (1861)
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.9
de.wikipedia, 'Graf von Saint-Germain'
Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'

stops.name: Schloss Louisenlund, near Guby: the tower laboratory
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1779 by the German Wikipedia. Coordinates corrected: Louisenlund stands at 54 deg 29' 35" N, 9 deg 41' 06" E in Guby, about six kilometres from the pool's pin, which fell north of the Schlei. The house was built 1772-1776 for Prince Charles as a gift for Princess Louise of Denmark and was newly finished when the count arrived. Month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: The prince installs him in a tower of the new house at Louisenlund, finished three years earlier as a gift for the princess, and equips him with an alchemical laboratory. In Paris that same season an engraver publishes his portrait with laudatory verse calling him a Prometheus. The Prometheus is in a tower on the Schlei, somewhere past sixty, grinding pigment. The two men work together on colours and metals, and set up a silk-dyeing venture down the water at Eckernforde.
suggested_refs: The 1783 copper engraving of the count, after a portrait from the d'Urfe collection, dedicated to the Comte de Milly

stops.name: Otte dye works, Kieler Strasse, Eckernforde
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1779-1784 by the Eckernforde city museum, which holds the local record of the venture and of the damp lodging blamed for his rheumatic attacks. The stop date opens the working period; month and day are not recorded and are defaulted.
stops.campa: The venture takes over the empty Otte factory on Kieler Strasse: vats, alloys, trials for a fast industrial colour that will hold in cloth and sell by the bolt. It never becomes a product. He is past sixty-five and lives on the premises, in the last of the five courts and workshops that have housed him, and the town remembers the lodging as damp. It gets the blame afterwards for the rheumatic attacks of his final years. The Eckernforde city museum keeps what is left of the local record.
suggested_refs: The Otte factory building on Kieler Strasse, Eckernforde
sources: museum-eckernfoerde.de, 'Abenteurer: Der Graf von St. Germain'

stops.name: Holstein, the initiation his enemies describe
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction resting on hostile pamphlet literature, the Memoires authentiques pour servir a l'histoire du comte de Cagliostro (1785), written to destroy its subject. A. E. Waite judged the evidentiary basis very thin. Cagliostro's own documented movements do not bring him to Holstein. Undated in every source; the year is an ordering device inside the Schleswig period.
stops.campa: Hostile pamphlet literature of 1785, written to destroy Cagliostro, has the count receive him somewhere in Holstein and initiate him into Egyptian Masonry, making the older adventurer master of the younger. Cagliostro's own documented movements do not bring him here. The two men are paired constantly in print from 1785 onward. A. E. Waite, sifting the story a century and a bit later, finds the evidence for it very thin, and no witness has ever been produced who was in the room.
suggested_refs: Memoires authentiques pour servir a l'histoire du comte de Cagliostro (1785)
A. E. Waite, 'Saint-Germain and Cagliostro'

stops.name: St. Nicolai Church, Eckernforde: the death and the private burial
stops.date_confidence: attested twice over: the Eckernforde church register, quoted through Louis Bobe in Cooper-Oakley p.63, gives death on 27 February 1784 and private entombment on 2 March; the Nicolai church accounts record the burial charge on 1 March 1784. The English Wikipedia and the Eckernforde museum corroborate both.
stops.campa: He dies on the twenty-seventh of February in Eckernforde and is buried privately in St. Nicolai on the second of March. The parish register enters him as the so-called Count of Saint-Germain and Weldon, joining the two names, and adds that further information about his person is not known. No birthplace, no age, no family is entered beside the names. The church accounts note the charge the next day: a tomb for thirty years at ten Reichsthaler, two more for the opening, twelve in all.
suggested_refs: The Eckernforde parish register and the Nicolai church account book, 1784
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.63
Wikipedia, 'Comte de Saint Germain'

stops.name: Eckernforde, the council calls the creditors
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the issuing body; the content is described differently by two sources. Cooper-Oakley p.63 gives a creditors' call with a deadline of 14 October and a clause about four years' residence in the country; the English Wikipedia describes the same 3 April proclamation as concerning the auction of his remaining effects. The 14 October deadline and the four-year clause rest on Cooper-Oakley alone and could not be corroborated.
stops.campa: On the third of April the mayor and council issue a public notice under both names, Saint-Germain and Weldon, calling anyone with a claim on the estate to present it, since the deceased had lived four years in the country and left no will and no known heir. The town, unable to settle the question of who he was, prints him under both names and lets the creditors choose. Cooper-Oakley gives the deadline as the fourteenth of October; the English account of the same proclamation describes it instead as the auction of his effects. No inventory of what was sold has been recovered.
suggested_refs: The Eckernforde municipal proclamation of 3 April 1784
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.63
Wikipedia, 'Count of St. Germain'

stops.name: Berlin, Biester answers the immortals
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1785 through Cooper-Oakley p.63, quoting Dr. Biester's notice in the Berlinische Monatschrift; the day is not given and is defaulted. Biester's own phrasing, that the count died two years ago in Danish Holstein, is loose by a year against the February 1784 register entry.
stops.campa: Fifteen months after the funeral, Dr. Biester of the Berlinische Monatschrift gives a hostile notice to the people who insist the count is still living, and states flatly that he died two years ago in Danish Holstein. He is out by a year: the Eckernforde register gives the twenty-seventh of February 1784. It is the first recorded attempt to answer the immortality story with a death record, and it is made by a man who has the date wrong. The correction does not take.
suggested_refs: Berlinische Monatschrift, June 1785
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.63

stops.name: Paris, the Convent of the Philalethes lists a dead man
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a posthumous claim. The assembly that opened in Paris on 15 February 1785 and sat until 26 May was the Convent des Philalethes, which invited 228 brothers including Saint-Martin; the Masonic source Cooper-Oakley cites, 'Freimaurer Bruderschaft in Frankreich' in Latomia vol. ii, p.9, points to France and not to Hanau. The pool attached this date to Wilhelmsbad, which met in 1782. Cooper-Oakley herself flags the conflict with the church record. Canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: Two hundred and twenty-eight brothers are invited to the assembly that opens in Paris on the fifteenth of February and sits until the twenty-sixth of May, Saint-Martin among the named. A Masonic source lists Saint-Germain among them as well. He has been in the ground at Eckernforde for eleven and a half months. Cooper-Oakley, who prints the claim, also prints the parish register and the burial charge, and lets the two stand against each other in the same book without choosing between them.
suggested_refs: The Convent des Philalethes, Paris, 15 February to 26 May 1785, and its list of invitations
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912), p.64
fr.wikipedia, 'Philalethes'

stops.name: Piazza San Marco, Venice: the sighting after the burial
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction and probable fabrication. The claim is that the Comte de Chalons met the count in the Place Saint-Marc in 1788, reported at second hand in the Souvenirs published in 1836 under the name of the Comtesse d'Adhemar; bibliographic scholarship attributes that book to Etienne-Leon de Lamothe-Langon, a documented manufacturer of historical memoirs. Month and day unknown and defaulted. The verses quoted here are footnoted by Cooper-Oakley to Adhemar vol. iv, pp.74-97, and dated by her own footnote to 1788; the ellipsis elides roughly fourteen lines.
stops.campa: The Comte de Chalons, coming back from an embassy, tells the Countess d'Adhemar that he has spoken with the count in the Place Saint-Marc in Venice, four years after the burial. The Souvenirs in which she says so were published in 1836 under her name and are attributed by bibliographers to Etienne-Leon de Lamothe-Langon, a professional manufacturer of historical memoirs. Nearly everything anyone repeats about Saint-Germain and the French Revolution comes out of that one book.
stops.quote: The time is fast approaching when imprudent France, / Surrounded by misfortune she might have spared herself, / Will call to mind such hell as Dante painted... At last, closing the abyss and born from a black tomb / There rises a young lily, more happy, and more fair.
stops.quote_source: Verses in a letter attributed to the count, in the Comtesse d'Adhemar, Souvenirs sur Marie-Antoinette (1836), vol. iv, pp.74-97, reproduced in Cooper-Oakley, pp.78-79 (1927 printing)
suggested_refs: Souvenirs sur Marie-Antoinette (1836) and the modern scholarship identifying Lamothe-Langon as its author
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912/1927), pp.63-64, 78-79
books.google.com, Souvenirs sur Marie-Antoinette (1836) volume record

stops.name: Paris, the letter to the Countess
stops.date_confidence: the wording is verbatim from Cooper-Oakley p.85 of the 1927 printing, footnoted to Adhemar vol. iv, pp.189-193 and signed in her text 'Comte de St.-Germain'. The date is corrected: the pool gave 1788, but Cooper-Oakley introduces the sequence as concerning the proscription of the Royalists in 1789 and the preceding letter names the murders of de Launay and Flesselles on 14 July 1789. The source itself is the disputed Lamothe-Langon forgery. Canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: The same book prints a note in his hand warning that the sun now setting is the last the monarchy will see, and dates the sequence to the summer the Bastille falls and the provost of the merchants is killed in the street. Cooper-Oakley's own text puts the surrounding letters in 1789, though the note is commonly reprinted under 1788. Almost everything France remembers of him is in these letters. They were composed some time before 1836, by a man who wrote historical memoirs for a living.
stops.quote: All is lost, Countess! This sun is the last which will set on the monarchy; tomorrow it will exist no more, chaos will prevail, anarchy unequalled. You know all I have tried to do to give affairs a different turn; I have been scorned; now it is too late.
stops.quote_source: Letter signed 'Comte de St.-Germain' in the Comtesse d'Adhemar, Souvenirs sur Marie-Antoinette (1836), vol. iv, pp.189-193, reproduced in Cooper-Oakley p.85 (1927 printing)
suggested_refs: The Adhemar Souvenirs, source of the entire French prophetic cycle
sources: Cooper-Oakley, The Comte de St. Germain (1912/1927), p.85

stops.name: Eckernforde, the grave under the storm flood
stops.date_confidence: attested: the gravestone in St. Nicolai was destroyed in the Baltic storm surge of 1872, per literaturland-sh.de, and the Eckernforde city museum states that the grave is no longer findable and that nothing marks it. The 1872 Ostseesturmflut struck on 12-13 November; the day here follows that event and is not separately given by the source. The 2009 hoax is dated 1 April 2009 by the same page.
stops.campa: The Baltic storm surge of November 1872 takes the coast of Schleswig and the low ground of the town, and the gravestone in St. Nicolai is destroyed with it. After that nobody can say where in the church he lies. The town museum states plainly that the grave is not findable and that nothing marks it. In 2009 a local paper announced on the first of April that divers had brought the stone up out of the harbour. People came to the church to look at it.
suggested_refs: The Ostseesturmflut of 1872 and its damage to the Schleswig coast
sources: literaturland-sh.de, 'Saint-Germain, Graf von'

stops.name: Mount Shasta, California: the Master on the mountain
stops.date_confidence: religious testimony, not a historical claim; the encounter is dated to August 1930 by the English Wikipedia and narrated in Guy Ballard's Unveiled Mysteries (1934). Steiner's identification of the count with Christian Rosenkreuz is dated 27 September 1911 and was delivered at Neuchatel, not in Germany as the pool's chronology has it; rsarchive.org returned HTTP 403 and the primary lecture text could not be checked. Blavatsky's naming of Master Rakoczi runs from Isis Unveiled (1877) and a Theosophist article of May 1881, and is absent from blavatsky.journey.json.
stops.campa: Blavatsky had already made him a Master under the name Rakoczi; Rudolf Steiner told an audience in 1911 that the count had been Christian Rosenkreuz in an earlier body. In August 1930 Guy Ballard, writing afterwards as Godfre Ray King, says a man on the slope of this mountain handed him a cup of liquid and named himself Saint Germain. The I AM Activity dates itself from that walk. When the federal government prosecutes Ballard's family for mail fraud, the Supreme Court holds that no jury may be asked whether a religious claim is true.

stops.name: Troyes, the manuscript that carries his name
stops.date_confidence: the manuscript, MS 2400 in the Troyes library, is late eighteenth century and undated; the attribution rests on a pasted bookseller's note and a pencil note tying it to Cagliostro. The stop date is that of Manly P. Hall's Los Angeles edition, The Most Holy Trinosophia (1933), which carried the attribution into modern circulation; the Dictionary of Gnosis and Western Esotericism calls the text pseudo-Saint-Germain. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: A ninety-nine leaf illuminated manuscript of hermetic and cabalistic matter sits in the library at Troyes with a bookseller's slip pasted into it attributing the work to the Comte de Saint-Germain, and a pencil note tying it to Cagliostro, who is said to have owned the only copy. Manly P. Hall publishes it at Los Angeles in 1933 as The Most Holy Trinosophia, and the attribution travels with it into every occult catalogue since. The Dictionary of Gnosis and Western Esotericism calls the text pseudo-Saint-Germain. The manuscript is not signed.
